articles.title: Jaishankar meets Azerbaijan President, Foreign Minister as India attempts reset of ties
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar on Friday (October 23, 2026) met Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev in Baku and said the visit charted a “pathway” for the future of the bilateral ties. The meeting comes more than a year after relations between India and Azerbaijan deteriorated over the latter’s opposition to India’s Operation Sindoor against Pakistan.

Mr. Jaishankar also met his counterpart Jayhun Bayramov, who said the two countries had “different view points on different issues” earlier, but highlighted new areas of cooperation like energy, and tourism after what he described as a “fruitful discussion”.

“We have common interest in really promoting peace and progress and prosperity. And threats like terrorism, conflict, and instability are our common enemies,” Mr. Jaishankar said in his remarks to the media after the meeting with Mr. Bayramov.

“Delighted to welcome the External Affairs Minister of India, Dr. S. Jaishankar, to exchange views on the current state and prospects of Azerbaijan-India relations, including political dialogue, trade and investment, energy, tourism and cultural ties,” said Mr. Bayramov, emphasising “continued dialogue and exploration of opportunities for cooperation in areas of mutual interest”.

“Our talks charted a pathway forward for our relationship. Agreed to deepen political consultations, exchange visits, enhance economic activities, build connectivity and foster people-to-people ties,” Mr. Jaishankar said. He also extended India’s support to the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia, saying that “India welcomes the initialling of the peace agreement by the leaders of Armenia and Azerbaijan last August. We hope this will lead to the establishment of lasting peace. India’s position is very clear: disputes must be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.”

The statement is the first major conciliatory step from the Indian side since Azerbaijan had expressed concern over the India-initiated Operation Sindoor of May 2025. Azerbaijan Foreign Ministry had, on May 7, 2025, condemned the Indian strikes against Pakistan-based terror targets. “We condemn military attacks against the Islamic Republic of Pakistan that killed and injured several civilians,” the Azerbaijani Ministry had said.

Azerbaijan has also been vocal on the Kashmir issue at the international level, often calling for its “resolution”. Azerbaijan participated in the meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Contact Group on Kashmir on September 22 this year, where Mr. Bayramov said his country sought “peaceful resolution of the Jammu and Kashmir issue in accordance with the norms and principles of international law, the UN Charter, and the relevant resolutions of the UN Security Council.”

Mr. Bayramov in his remarks on Friday (October 23, 2026) downplayed the differences between the two sides and said they have maintained regular contact through multilateral as well as bilateral formats. “We have touched upon a number of issues. I believe Azerbaijan-India relations are on their way to developing to a higher level,” said Mr. Bayramov.

Despite past issues in ties, Mr. Bayramov on Friday highlighted Indian investments in the energy sector of Azerbaijan, spoke about the expanding air connectivity with India, and the growing presence of the Indian community, especially students, in his country. “It is no secret, we had different view point on different issues (but) today we had very long and positive and fruitful discussion,” Mr. Bayramov said.

Mr. Jaishankar’s visit to Baku is the first bilateral visit by an Indian External Affairs Minister in eight years. The late External Affairs Minister Sushma Swaraj had visited Azerbaijan in April 2018 for a Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) Ministerial meeting.

Mr. Bayramov in his remark reminded that India and Azerbaijan have remained connected through NAM mechanism and that he had met Mr. Jaishankar on the sidelines of the NAM ministerial meeting in Kampala, Uganda, in January 2024. These interactions had paved the ground for a meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and the Azerbaijani President, Mr. Aliyev, at the SCO summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyz Republic, last month.

Official sources here described the remarks from both sides on Friday as a sign of “diplomatic reset” as India expects to exert pressure on Turkiye and Pakistan by drawing Azerbaijan close. Azerbaijan is also understandably seeking India’s support to join the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO). Ministry of External Affairs Spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal told the media that the discussion on this matter will be held within the SCO grouping.

articles.title: Talks between Ladakh groups, MHA fail to resume amid rift over govt. proposal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The proposed talks between the Union Home Ministry and representatives from Ladakh failed to take place on Thursday (October 22, 2026) amid growing differences among civil society groups over the Centre’s draft proposal for the Union Territory.

Leh’s civil society groups, particularly the Leh Apex Body (LAB) and the Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA), had termed the 32-page draft, which proposes a new governance structure for Ladakh, “a departure from the earlier promises”.

Ladakh has been witnessing frequent street protests since it was carved out as a Union Territory in 2019 from the erstwhile State of Jammu and Kashmir. Since then, the region has been demanding the Statehood and inclusion in the Sixth Schedule (that allows autonomy for certain tribal areas).

A sub-committee of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), mandated to talk with Ladakh representatives, was scheduled to meet on October 22 in New Delhi to further discuss the 32-page draft shared with the LAB and KDA on October 15 in Leh. However, the talks did not take place.

The Civil Society Forum of Ladakh (CSFL), a Leh-based civil society group, is projecting itself as a new stakeholder in the issue. “This forum notes with regret that despite several rounds of talks and consensus arrived at between the Government of India (GoI) and representatives of the LAB and KDA, the same consensus is being consistently disregarded through shifting goalposts and delaying tactics. This has created a trust deficit and is against the larger interest of Ladakh,” said the members of the CSFL in a joint statement.

The CSFL comprises BJP leader and ex-Member of Parliament Thupstan Chhewang, ex-chief executive councillor of the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council-Leh (LAHDC-Leh) Rigzen Spalbar; ex-legislator Tsering Samphel, representatives of Thiksey and Thuksey Rinpoche, and also members of the Ladakh Buddhist Association (LBA).

It urged Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah “to take note of the ground reality”. “The LAB and KDA no longer represent the inclusive voice of all districts,” the forum said. It also appealed to the Centre to hold panchayat elections and “enhance powers of hill councils in all eight districts till Union Territory-level constitutional settlement is reached”.

“This forum observes with deep concern that the original agenda adopted by LAB for constitutional safeguards for land, jobs, culture and environment stands hijacked. The dialogue is now dominated by one individual (climate activist) Sonam Wangchuk and KDA, compromising the genuine interests of districts and the Buddhist community. What should have been a dialogue for an amicable solution has been converted into a process of confrontation with the GoI, which is not in the interest of Ladakh,” it said.

The forum also seconded Ladakh Chief Secretary Ashish Kundra’s recent statement that “formation of a UT-level democratic political institution with full constitutional safeguards under Article 371-like provisions is a complex constitutional exercise, which will require time, detailed drafting, and Parliamentary process”. “In view of consistent opposing and delaying tactics adopted by the LAB and the KDA, such a solution seems far-fetched in the near future,” said the forum.

It underlined that only elected hill councils in every district “can give real protection to land, culture, natural resources, trading, recruitment, tourism and mining licences”. “Safeguards under Article 371 and genuine powers to LAHDCs will ensure no outsider can buy land, get a job or licence without concurrence of that District Council,” it added.

The forum said that without panchayats for the last six years, village-level development, MGNREGA, and funds are stalled. “This is against the spirit of the 73rd Amendment. Elections will bring genuine public representatives to the fore, not self-styled leaders, and will create authentic interlocutors for future talks with the Gol,” said the forum.

Meanwhile, LAB co-chairman Chering Dorjay Lakrook issued a counter statement to Mr. Chewang-led civil society group’s allegations. Mr. Lakrook said he made a call on the morning of October 20 to Mr. Kundra and sought confirmation of the meeting scheduled for October 22 with the Ministry, “so that the issues could be discussed comprehensively and directly”.

articles.title: IndusInd Bank posts profit of ₹1,242 crores in Q2; asset quality improvement and interest income drives growth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: IndusInd Bank Limited posted a net profit of ₹1,242 crore for the quarter ended September, up 20% sequentially and trimming net loss of ₹437 for the same quarter in the preceding year. The bank had incurred net loss for the same period in previous year due to an increase in microfinance provisioning and write-offs.

The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago. Sequentially, interest income declined by 2%. NII for half year (H1FY27) rose to ₹9,254, up 2.3% on year.

Asset quality of the bank improved substantially, with gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio at 2.73% compared to 3.60% on year and net NPA declining to 0.83% from 1.04% in Q2FY26. However, the net interest margin of the bank slipped to 3.23% from 3.32% a year ago.

Net revenue of the bank for the period rose to ₹6,817 crores compared to ₹6,00 crores a year. A decline in operating expenses also helped push the bottom-line numbers, with expenses slipping to ₹3,943 crores in July-Septemeber from ₹4,013 crore for the same period last year.
Deposits of the bank rose 10% year-on-year to ₹4.28 crores. Advances of the bank for the period stood at 3.63 crores.
IndusInd held provisions of $9,012 crore as of September 30, with the provision coverage ratio at 70%.

IndusInd Bank raised nearly $3.5 billion via the Reserve Bank of India’s special window for foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) account, which was impacted the contraction in NIM. The bank said recovery in margin related to FCNR-B is expected over the next two quarters.

“Q2 reflects the growing strength of the IndusInd Bank franchise and the progress we have made in rebuilding momentum across the business. Our Q2 results demonstrate that the growth has strengthened, profitability has improved, asset quality trends remain encouraging, and our funding profile is becoming more granular and resilient,” Rajiv Anand, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of IndusInd Bank said.

The bank also informed the exchanges on Friday (October 23, 2026) that the Board of Directors of the lender has appointed Priyanka Sinha as an Additional Director in the category of Non-Executive Independent Director for a period of four consecutive years, till October 22, 2030.

Speaking to the media at post-earnings conference call, the bank said it remains confident of reaching a 1% exit return on assets for FY27. Bank also expects loans growth momentum to continue driven by retail and wholesale lending. Shares of IndusInd Bank Ltd closed at ₹835.00 on Friday, down 1.76%, on the BSE.

articles.title: Government to modify labour survey to capture gig economy, unpaid household workers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Union government has decided to change the design and structure of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) to track digital platform workers and capture engagement in unpaid household, caregiving, volunteer, and trainee work. The PLFS will also include additional questions to measure labour underutilisation.

According to a press release and concept note issued in New Delhi on Friday (October 23, 2026), the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), has proposed modifications to the PLFS sampling design starting January 2027. The survey schedule will also change.
The Ministry has invited comments and suggestions from policymakers, researchers, academic institutions, and the public within 15 days from Friday.

A separate Second Stage Stratum (SSS) will be introduced in the PLFS to identify households with at least one digital platform worker. An additional entry will be added to the questionnaire to determine whether any member of the household has engaged in digital platform work during the specified reference period.

“There will be four SSSs in rural areas and five in urban areas, with 14 households canvassed in each selected First Stage Unit (FSU). This revision in SSS formation is expected to improve the coverage of digital platform workers and facilitate more comprehensive data collection on this emerging segment of the labour market,” the press release said.

According to the concept note, a large proportion of women in India spend considerable time on unpaid household and caregiving activities, such as cooking, cleaning, childcare, and caring for elderly, sick, or disabled family members. “While such activities contribute significantly to household well-being and facilitate the participation of other household members in paid employment, they have not been measured separately in PLFS until now,” it noted, adding that specific questions will be incorporated to capture engagement in own-use production of goods, unpaid household and caregiving activities, volunteer work, and unpaid trainee work.

Additionally, the criteria for sample allocation and stratification have been updated based on the experience of the previous two years. “These revisions are expected to improve the efficiency of sample allocation and stratification and ensure better representation of population variations, which in turn will minimise operational difficulties during sample selection,” the press release said.

articles.title: Bharat Petroleum’s net profit dips amid volatile crude prices in Q2
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Bharat Petroleum’s standalone net profits in the September-end quarter fell 22.5% on a year-over-year basis as volatile crude prices impacted margins following the reignited conflict in West Asia.
The Mumbai-headquartered refiner’s net profit declined to ₹4,993.17 crore in the reported quarter compared to ₹6,442.5 crore in the same period last year.
The state-owned oil-marketing company’s cost of materials consumed soared 44.2% during the period to ₹74,969 crore.
Revenues increased about 30% on a year-over-year basis to more than ₹1.58 lakh crore.
The refiners’ physical performance reported an uptick. It rose 6% during the mentioned period to 10.41 million metric tonnes (MMT).
Its peer Hindustan Petroleum had reported a 9% decline in standalone net profits on Thursday.
Delhi-headquartered peer Indian Oil is scheduled to post their September-end financial results on October 30.

articles.title: Crude oil sourcing presently volatile; procuring more on landed basis: HPCL Chief
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Crude oil sourcing at present is very volatile and unpredictable, and Hindustan Petroleum is procuring more on a delivered basis than free-on-board (FOB) and term contracts, Vikas Kaushal, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) of the state-owned oil-marketing company told analysts in an investor call on Friday (October 23, 2026).
Purchases on delivered basis entail the seller bearing the cost of shipping the oil and associated risks until it reaches the buyer’s port or facility.

“All I can say if you look at crude premiums and landed cost: there are times when there are premiums and there are times when you can even pick it up at discounts. It is a very ‘Wild West’ right now” he said.

articles.title: Net FDI at $3.3 billion in September 2026, positive for third consecutive month
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: Net foreign direct investment (FDI) remained positive for the third consecutive month in August 2026, with inflows exceeding outflows by $3.3 billion, according to the latest data by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). This was driven by robust inflows even as outward investment by Indian companies fell.

“FDI flows continued to remain robust in August 2026, supported by strong gross inflows and moderation in outward FDI,” the RBI said in its monthly Bulletin. “Communication, miscellaneous services and manufacturing received more than two-thirds of the FDI inflows.”

Net FDI, which is the difference between the total direct investment coming in and the total going out, was positive in seven out of the last eight months. This is a significant turnaround from the five consecutive months of negative net FDI India saw during August-December 2025.

The data shows that gross FDI into India, or the total that entered the country as direct investment, stood at $11.1 billion in August 2026, which was 24% lower than in the previous month, but nearly 68% higher than in August last year.
“The U.S., Singapore and Mauritius were the major source countries, accounting for about 72% of FDI inflows,” the report noted.

Total outflows increased marginally to $7.7 billion in August 2026 as compared to $7.2 billion in July, and $6.7 billion in August 2025. However, in this, the driver was the repatriation by foreign companies operating in India rather than outward investment by Indian companies.

“Outward FDI flows moderated in August with more than half being directed towards Singapore, the Netherlands, and the U.S,” the RBI said. “The major sectors of outward FDI were agriculture & mining, financial, insurance & business services, and manufacturing — together accounting for more than two-thirds of the outward flows.”

Remittances increased to $5.8 billion in August 2026, which was nearly 52% higher than in July, and 28% higher than in August last year. This was largely balanced out by a fall in outward FDI, which fell to $1.9 billion. This was more than 43% lower than in July 2026 and 11% lower than in August last year.
Looking at the longer time-period of April-August 2026, the RBI noted that gross inward FDI and net FDI flows were both higher during this period.

A slowdown in the pace of outward FDI along with sustained higher gross FDI inflows supported net FDI flows,” the RBI said. “Financial services, communication services, computer services and manufacturing accounted for around 73% of total FDI equity inflows during April-August 2026.”

articles.title: Data suggests broad-based increase in food prices: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data collected by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for October (till 19th), suggest a broad-based increase in food prices, said RBI officials in the October edition of RBI Bulletin, which was released on Friday (October 23, 2026).

“Among cereals, rice and wheat prices continued to increase. Prices of major pulses also went up sequentially. Edible oil prices also recorded a slow and broad-based increase, led by mustard and palm oil,” they wrote in the ‘State of the Economy’ article.
Among vegetables, while potato prices declined and the pace of onion price increases dropped, tomato prices picked up, they added.

Surprisingly, inflation in rural areas has been getting higher than that in urban areas. Inflation stood at 4.9% and 6.1%, respectively, in urban and rural areas in September. In August, urban and rural inflation stood at 4.3% and 5.2% respectively, the officials stated.
ALSO WATCH The battle against inflation is entering a tougher phase: What it means for you

The majority of States/UTs recorded inflation in the range of 4-6% in September. Inflation ranged from 2.9% to 6.9% across states/UTs. States like Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry recorded inflation in excess of 6% across both rural and urban areas, they pointed out.

Stating that WPI inflation recorded its first double-digit rate in the new series (Base 2022-23) at 11.4% in September 2026, rising from 9.9% in August, reflecting a broad-based increase in prices, they said industrial and farm input costs remained elevated.
Inflation in the Output Producer Price Index surged to 11.4% in September 2026 from 9.8% in August, led by manufacturing products, and mining & quarrying, they said.
As per the article headline, CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities, calling for a commensurate change in the monetary policy stance.
“The external headwinds are also being dealt with a slew of regulatory measures by the Reserve Bank to curb speculative activity in foreign exchange market,” they stated.

“Strong inflows under FCNR(B) swap window augmented reserves. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) and remittance flows strengthened in August. With strong exports growth, the trade deficit narrowed in September,” they added.

The headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rose to a 23-month high of 5.5% (YoY) in September from 4.8% in August, driven by a broad-based increase in food, fuel and core (CPI excluding food and fuel) components.

articles.title: Rescuers search for survivors after deadly earthquake in China’s Tibet region
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Rescuers combed through a remote area in the Chinese region of Tibet on Friday (October 23, 2026) after a magnitude 7 earthquake that killed at least 16 people, injured 54 and collapsed hundreds of homes, according to Chinese state media.

The disaster struck Nagqu, a city north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa, which is some 4,800 meters (5,249 yards) above sea level, on Thursday (October 22, 2026). At least 339 homes collapsed, and officials told journalists they were concerned about further building collapses from aftershocks, as well as casualties from rockslides.

Search and rescue efforts are complicated by the geography and low temperatures, officials said. As of Friday afternoon (October 23, 2026), rescuers had done three rounds of searches, going through each household, and each village, said Dunzhu, the acting mayor of Nagqu city, said in a press conference.

More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies, including 2,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,400 tents and 2,000 folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.

The U.S. Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time on Thursday (October 22, 2026), with its epicentre 191 kilometres (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu. It put the earthquake’s depth at 18 kilometers (11 miles).
ALSO WATCH Watch: Rescue operations continue in Tibet after 7.0-magnitude earthquake
The U.S. agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitudes between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10 kilometers (6 miles), according to its website.

China’s official news agency Xinhua said on Friday (October 23, 2026) that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities have taken emergency action to halt trains passing through the region.

The earthquake also caused rockfalls that have forced local authorities to close a section of National Highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.
Intermittent snows are expected in the earthquake region over the next three days, Xinhua said.

Chinese President Xi Jinping called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work, issuing instructions Friday morning. The Chinese leader does so only in major disasters and accidents.

articles.title: Trump says will talk to Musk if Ukraine's Starlink not fixed
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday (October 23, 2026) that he would speak to tech tycoon Elon Musk if there are still problems with Ukraine's military-grade version of the Starlink service.
"If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out," Mr. Trump told reporters at the White House after Ukraine said it was still having problems with the Starshield communications platform.
Asked if he had contacted Mr. Musk to restore access, Mr. Trump replied: "I have not spoken to him. I might have to, but I have not. I've heard it was fixed, but if it's not, I'll speak to him."
Mr. Trump had said on Thursday (October 22, 2026) that Mr. Musk, whose SpaceX is behind the Starshield system, had restored access.

The billionaire President on Friday (October 23, 2026) also rejected suggestions that Musk had too much power over a system that is vital for Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion, now in its fifth year. "I don't think he does," he said. "Elon will never do anything wrong. I know him very well, he is a fair person."
Mr. Trump has had a complicated relationship with Ms. Musk, who led the cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year before falling out with the president.
The pair appeared to have made up again in recent months, with South African-born Musk attending a state banquet for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September.

articles.title: Kremlin says a first tanker of Russian diesel sets sail for U.S. despite Ukraine's protests
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the United States under a new import agreement has set sail, the Kremlin said Friday (October 23, 2026), two weeks after President Donald Trump said he struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin despite Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
“The first oil tanker has sailed off to customers, and regular supplies will continue,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said without elaborating.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said earlier this week that the first shipment would amount to 40,000 tons of diesel, according to Russia's Interfax news agency.
Marine intelligence firm Kpler said the vessel was signalling it was headed to New York to arrive Nov. 7 and would be the first Russian diesel delivery to the United States since July 2023.
The abrupt reversal of U.S. sanctions policy on Russia over its invasion of its neighbour was seen as an attempt by Mr. Trump to address high fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections.
The diesel shipment of 40,000 tons amounts to around 300,000 barrels, or about 7% of the roughly 4 million barrels of diesel the U.S. economy consumes in a single day.

The import agreement, which Mr. Trump says foresees millions more tons of Russian diesel reaching the U.S. in coming months, is unlikely to make a dent in painfully high prices at the pump or elsewhere, energy policy experts say.

Russia's diesel production has come under strain from repeated Ukrainian long-range drone strikes on its oil refineries. The attacks caused fuel shortages, which have now eased. Mr. Trump last month asked Kyiv to stop the attacks.
The U.S. diesel decision caused alarm and dismay in Ukraine, which has pleaded with foreign countries to tighten sanctions on Moscow and deny it revenue for its invasion launched in February 2022.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Mr. Trump's decision “a weak decision by strong partners.”

The diesel agreement was a sudden policy reversal, coming just weeks after Mr. Trump signed into law a sweeping sanctions package that directed him to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas. He later put the measures on hold.
The development is the latest twist in the at-times volatile relationship between Mr. Trump and Mr. Zelenskyy, which in recent weeks has reached a new low.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine agree to Oleshky ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump, White House says
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: U.S. first lady Melania Trump has secured ​a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city of Oleshky, ‌which will begin on October 29, the White House ​said on Friday (October 23, 2026).
Residents of the southern Ukrainian town, ⁠occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis.

“Both nations agreed to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for ‌humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway,” a White House ‌statement said.

The development comes as Melania Trump’s husband, President Donald ‌Trump, ⁠pressures Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reach an agreement with ⁠Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, which began when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
Melania Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children ​seized by Russia during ‌the war returned to their families.

“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently ‌need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water,” Melania Trump ​said in the statement.

The ceasefire will allow non-military teams from both countries to visit residents in their ⁠homes and coordinate transportation for those wishing to evacuate to either Russia or Ukraine, with an unnamed American media organisation accompanying the teams ‌to document the process, the first lady said.
Newsmax , a right-leaning news outlet, said in a report that its cameras would be granted “exclusive access to document the effort.”

Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, has a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people — primarily elderly residents, along with about 50 children — down from roughly 24,000 ‌before the war, the White House said. About 90% of the city was ​flooded following the destruction of the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White House.
The statement said Melania Trump and ⁠her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms ⁠of the localised ceasefire.

“Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. ‌I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” Melania Trump said.

articles.title: Casualties feared as multi-storey building collapses in Nairobi
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: A multi-storey building collapsed mid-construction in the Kenyan capital on Friday (October 23, 2026), the Red Cross said, with reports from local media of casualties and looting at the site.

Videos spreading online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building -- thought to have been around 18 storeys high -- came down in a densely populated business and residential area of Eastleigh.
AFP journalists at the scene saw the building had been reduced to a pile of rubble as a small number of search and rescue teams arrived on the scene.
“There were some businesses in the basement, and workers who were busy building,” said local resident Abdi Aziz, 25.
“But as it was (the Friday prayer), a lot of them were at the mosque. I think few people died because no one was living there,” he told AFP .
Asked if he could see obvious flaws in the construction process, he said: “Everyone rushes to build in this neighbourhood.”
Local media reported looting and possible casualties trapped beneath the rubble, with images showing large crowds gathered at the site immediately after the incident, which happened around lunchtime.
AFP saw police use tear gas to disperse crowds gathering near the site.
Rescue operations had yet to begin when AFP arrived, with the site hemmed in by high-rise buildings, complicating efforts.

Nairobi is undergoing a rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings appearing all over the city, particularly in Eastleigh which is known for its busy market areas and as a hub for the Somali community.
There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.
An audit of almost 15,000 buildings by the National Building Inspectorate found that 4.8% were very dangerous, 72.3% were classified as unsafe, the report said.

fullParagraphs: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Friday (October 23, 2026) that he would speak to tech tycoon Elon Musk if there are still problems with Ukraine's military-grade version of the Starlink service.
"If there is a problem, I will get it straightened out," Mr. Trump told reporters at the White House after Ukraine said it was still having problems with the Starshield communications platform.

Mr. Trump had said on Thursday (October 22, 2026) that Mr. Musk, whose SpaceX is behind the Starshield system, had restored access.

The billionaire President on Friday (October 23, 2026) also rejected suggestions that Musk had too much power over a system that is vital for Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion, now in its fifth year. "I don't think he does," he said. "Elon will never do anything wrong. I know him very well, he is a fair person."
Mr. Trump has had a complicated relationship with Ms. Musk, who led the cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year before falling out with the president.
The pair appeared to have made up again in recent months, with South African-born Musk attending a state banquet for Chinese President Xi Jinping at the White House in September.

articles.title: Elon Musk's political baggage clouds prospects for SpaceX-Tesla deal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: A possible merger between Elon Musk ’s rocket ​company SpaceX and carmaker Tesla may face bigger obstacles from politics than from regulation, drawing scrutiny in Beijing and potentially igniting a battle between US President Donald Trump ‌and the Democrats.

Musk revived speculation about a tie-up this week, calling a combination “a good idea” and confirming that ​committees at both companies were reviewing a potential deal, a step toward what could become the largest merger in history ⁠and create a company worth about $3.5 trillion.

But a merger would also unite one of the US government’s most important aerospace and defense contractors with one of the most China-exposed major American manufacturers — a combination likely to raise questions about national security risks both in Washington and in Beijing.
Those concerns are unlikely to derail a deal, ‌analysts said, but they would likely leave the combined company exposed to years of political wrangling and pressure from both sides of the Pacific.

Tesla’s China operations, they said, could become a source of leverage for Beijing in any future dispute with ‌Washington, while a Democratic takeover of the US House of Representatives in next month’s midterm elections could subject the deal to congressional investigations and ‌political ⁠maneuvering.
Democrats immediately raised concerns about the deal’s implications, signaling their intent to turn the merger into a political flashpoint ahead ⁠of the November 3 midterms.

“If Elon Musk moves forward with the merger of Tesla and SpaceX, the deal would carry real risks that antitrust enforcers across the world would scrutinize,” said US Senator Cory Booker, a New Jersey Democrat who sits on both the Judiciary and Foreign Relations committees.

He added that he was prepared to conduct oversight of ​any deal: “When one person controls the infrastructure that governments and militaries ‌depend on, his business decisions become national security decisions, too.”
Musk could seek to address concerns by limiting how closely the two companies are integrated.

The greater threat to the deal may come later, however, if a future administration takes a harder line on the relationship between Tesla and a company increasingly tied to US national security, analysts said.
“A merger agreement would involve pledges of limits to the connections between SpaceX ‌and Tesla,” said Derek Scissors, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute.

“I don’t think the Trump administration would enforce ​these limits. However, the next administration could certainly begin to scrutinize a merged entity. This may be the biggest risk to a deal - that it could get unwound in 2029.”

articles.title: Airbnb sets down rules to stop hosts from forcing guests to clean homes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Airbnb, a company that facilitates travel accommodation agreements between private property owners and visitors, introduced a new rule that restrains hosts from making their guests perform too many household chores before they leave.

Airbnb hosts, as they are called, are allowed to set certain rules and requirements for the upkeep of their homes and apartments. For example, they could require guests to strip the bedsheets after their visit, take their trash to designated areas, do laundry, sweep floors, or run a dishwashing cycle.
Airbnb guests and hosts rate and review each other based on their experience, which can affect their standing when hosting future guests or visiting other Airbnb properties.
However, Airbnb guests have for years complained that, on top of being forced to carry out onerous household chores while on vacation, many Airbnb property hosts charge extravagant cleaning fees.
Airbnb has recently settled the debate, by stating in plain language that hosts must be “reasonable” and not use their guests as cleaners.

“For example, hosts are generally not allowed to: Ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes,” stated one of the rules in Airbnb’s help centre webpage.
The update has sparked a social media frenzy. Many guests reacted with relief, recounting anecdotes of being forced to do laundry and wash dishes while on holiday—on top of paying a cleaning fee.

Meanwhile, many Airbnb hosts lashed out against the updated rule, pointing out that Airbnb guests could stay at hotels or agree to higher fees if they did not want to do a few light cleaning tasks after their stay. For their part, a number of guests argued that Airbnb prices were almost on par with hotel booking fees—and also required the guest to work while on holiday.
Several hosts found the new rule confusing and felt that more flexibility was required.

“My main issue is it’s letting me ask people to load the dishwasher but I can’t ask them to start it. It’s a weird line to draw when the extra effort is 10 seconds (pop a pod in, press start),” stated one user on a Reddit forum for Airbnb hosts.
Other users pointed out that requiring guests to tidy up as a checkout requirement should not replace professional cleaning or home maintenance services between guests.
“Unless there is a dishwasher, guest should not be doing the dishes. Do you want to eat off dishes that a stranger washed in a hurry?” observed another Reddit user.

articles.title: How is air pollution in Delhi-NCR ahead of winter?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The story so far: As the air quality of Delhi worsened to the ‘poor’ category in the national capital, the Commission for Air Quality Management in NCR and adjoining areas (CAQM) on Wednesday (October 21, 2026) announced Stage 1 of the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) in Delhi and the National Capital Regio n (NCR) to bring down the pollution.

Every winter, air pollution spikes in Delhi-NCR and many parts of the larger Indo-Gangetic Plains, mainly due to meteorological factors such as lower wind speeds and a drop in temperature. Also, pollution from stubble burning during October and November, and bursting of firecrackers during the festive season add to existing pollution from vehicles and dust, worsening the air quality.

The GRAP or Graded Response Action Plan , is a set of short-term emergency measures to reduce air pollution and is divided into four stages. The CAQM announces the different stages, depending on the level of pollution recorded or forecast for the near future.

Whenever the CAQM announces GRAP, it directs State governments to implement the restrictions with “immediate effect” in entire Delhi and also in the NCR districts of Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, and Rajasthan. The restrictions will come into effect on the ground when respective State governments pass orders to implement them.
As per law, the State governments are bound to implement directions of the CAQM and the Commission can initiate legal action against officers not following its directions.

The GRAP was first notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in January, 2017, pursuant to Supreme Court directions to provide for graded measures corresponding to different levels of air quality.

Initially, the GRAP was implemented by the EPCA (Environmental Pollution (Prevention and Control) Authority), which was formed in 1998 by the Supreme Court and was responsible for the management and coordination on air pollution in Delhi and the NCR.
But the EPCA was not backed by a statute and experts had raised the issue that it lacked the teeth to act against authorities which did not follow its orders.

In 2021, the CAQM replaced the EPCA and since then it has been implementing the GRAP. Over the years, at times after coming under attack of the Supreme Court, the GRAP has gone through multiple revisions, making it more stringent.
Most of the actions under Stage 1 are directing authorities to strictly implement existing norms related to air pollution.

The four stages of GRAP are: Stage I – ‘Poor’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI ranging between 201-300), Stage II – ‘Very Poor’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI ranging between 301-400), Stage III – ‘Severe’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI ranging between 401-450), Stage IV – ‘Severe +’ Air Quality (Delhi AQI > 450).
Though the GRAP can be imposed any time during the year, the higher stages of GRAP are mostly invoked during winter as air quality deteriorates.

fullParagraphs: The Hindu is hosting a webinar on the theme ‘Modern Day Tips for Posture’. The webinar will be held on Sunday, October 25, 2026, from 11.30 a.m. to 12.30 p.m.

With long hours spent sitting at desks, using digital devices and working in fixed positions, posture and spine health have become important aspects of everyday health. The webinar will explore how daily habits, workplace ergonomics and physical inactivity affect the spine, and discuss practical ways to prevent and manage common problems such as back pain, neck pain and stiffness.

The discussion will cover the impact of prolonged sitting and poor posture on the spine and joints, the importance of movement and exercise, and simple ergonomic adjustments that can be made at home and at work. It will also examine how to distinguish everyday muscular discomfort from pain that may be associated with underlying joint or inflammatory conditions, common posture-related myths and mistakes, and when persistent back or neck pain warrants medical attention.

Panellists for the webinar include: Chetan. S. Pophale, consultant - spine surgeon, Apollo Speciality Hospitals, OMR, Chennai and A.B. Govindaraj, clinical director and senior consultant, department of orthopaedics, MGM Healthcare, Chennai. The discussion will be moderated by Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, The Hindu.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Fall of the centre: on the public discontent in France
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: When Emmanuel Macron came to power in 2017 , at age 39, he promised to keep extremist political forces at bay, build a new France through his ‘revolution’, rejuvenate economic growth, manage debt and create employment opportunities. Nine years later, with six months to go for France’s next presidential election, Mr. Macron, whose approval rating is at an abysmally low 15%, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu , who lacks a parliamentary majority, are struggling to restore order in a country battered by economic woes, street protests, violent riots and a surging far right. Even in France, where protests are part of the political culture, Saturday’s (October 17, 2026) riots and looting were a shock with at least 3,000 businesses and shops damaged. Municipal halls were attacked and buildings set on fire , including the 19 th -century Limoges town hall. Some 2,400 people were arrested and Prime Minister Lecornu called for local curfews . The trigger for the unrest was a move by Mr. Lecornu to pass budget proposals raising some taxes and freezing spending on social programmes. When school students hit the streets with demands for better educational facilities, the government responded with force and tear gas. But its heavy-handed response helped the student protest snowball into an anti-government movement, culminating in riots.

To understand the precarious situation France is in today, all one has to do is to look at the macroeconomic numbers. Growth remains sluggish with the economy estimated to expand by a mere 0.8% in 2026, while the unemployment rate stands at 8.3%. The core problem is the country’s public finances. France’s national debt stands at 120% of GDP, the third highest in the eurozone, after Greece and Italy. The French Treasury’s debt servicing bill is expected to reach about €60 billion in 2026. When Mr. Macron came to power, he reduced corporate taxes and sought to restrain public spending to stimulate growth. But growth remained sluggish while public debt ballooned. When protests gripped the country in 2018-19, he offered economic concessions, but with no long-term solutions to the structural problems the French economy was facing. In 2024, he called snap elections to blunt the far-right momentum. After the elections, he invited a leader from smaller blocs to form a government to keep the left-wing New Popular Front, the largest bloc, out of power, deepening the political crisis and weakening his position. This is Emmanuel Macron’s legacy. Worse, Marine Le Pen, leader of the far-right, anti-immigrant National Rally, could exploit the chaos and public anger to her benefit ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

articles.title: Unknown vulnerabilities: on the cybersecurity advisory by CERT-In
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The cybersecurity advisory by the Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has outlined two threat vectors vis-à-vis Indian commercial and government IT infrastructure: AI companies testing autonomous agents exceeding their designated operational constraints and bad actors weaponising open-source agentic AI tools for automated reconnaissance and exploitation. However, the organisations affected by recent breaches that the advisory was based on did not detect them: they came to light in the AI companies’ disclosures and CERT-In operations. Aside from developers allowing experimental systems to act outside their authorised bounds, the advisory highlights two problems for India — existing arrangements focus on cybersecurity incidents after they are revealed; and the implicated organisations being found under-prepared for the DPDP Act — to be enforced from 2027, including steep penalties on entities not maintaining reasonable safeguards against breaches. While CERT-In observed or received reports of 29.4 lakh incidents in 2025, it does not routinely publish postmortem analyses and is exempt from the RTI Act. As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.

AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. Finally, the government should also review the exemption for CERT-In from the RTI Act as such a sweeping exemption is unnecessary for effective cyber-defence.

As a result, public accountability is also weak: CERT-In found that the AI agents and/or bad actors exploited vulnerabilities, including exposed passwords, that are known security problems separate from AI agents’ abilities.
• AI companies and labs have made several disclosures this year of agents unexpectedly breaching real-world infrastructure worldwide during testing. For India, however, the legal boundaries specified by the IT Act 2000 leave open an accountability gap for autonomous agents without the backing of human intentions. A more specific lacuna is that while CERT-In requires an organisation to report an intrusion within six hours, many organisations remain incapable of, or unwilling to, discover it. The reporting deadline itself has not ensured detection. Overall, the national cybersecurity landscape is fragmented across a pastiche of enforceable requirements in some domains, advisory technical standards in others, and narrow AI-specific accountability in yet others. As human and autonomous threat actors become more sophisticated, India needs to leapfrog to a landscape with enforceable risk-based requirements for both testing and defending against autonomous agents; better spotting unauthorised access, especially in the public sector; and a legal safe-harbour for security research conducted in good faith, in line with CERT-In policy. CERT-In should also publish more information, anonymised where necessary, which includes remediation outcomes and whether the affected individuals were informed. Finally, the government should also review the exemption for CERT-In from the RTI Act as such a sweeping exemption is unnecessary for effective cyber-defence.
